opus-5.5.text:
Well, I should say up front that I was never one of the people who thought the whole concern was silly. I've known people in the rationalist and AI-alignment communities for a long time, I've read their arguments, and I always took seriously the basic point that if you build something much smarter than yourself, you'd better have thought hard about what it's going to want.

My skepticism was more about what to *do*. For years, when people said, "You should drop quantum computing and work on AI safety," my response was: okay, but what would I actually work on? What's the research program? In science, progress almost always comes from having some concrete thing you can poke at, a system you can run experiments on, a model that gives you feedback when you're wrong. When the "AI" in question was a hypothetical superintelligence that might exist decades from now, with an architecture nobody could specify, it felt like trying to design safety protocols for nuclear reactors before anyone had discovered fission. You could write philosophy papers, and some of that was valuable, but it wasn't clear to me how you'd know whether you were making progress or just going around in circles.

There's also a general wariness I have about arguments of the form "this cause has such enormous stakes that everything else you're doing is a rounding error." That style of reasoning can justify almost anything, and history is full of people who were absolutely certain that their particular apocalypse took priority over everything else. So I wanted to see the argument cash out in something more tangible than expected-value calculations with astronomically large numbers.

What changed for me was, frankly, GPT and the large language models. Suddenly there were actual systems, really impressive ones, that you could study, that did surprising things, that you could try to align or interpret or watermark or red-team. The problem went from being purely speculative to being something with an experimental side. That's a big part of why I was willing to take time away from quantum computing and spend a while working on this stuff. It wasn't that the philosophical arguments suddenly got more convincing; it was that the field finally had something you could get your hands on.

r001.rationale: He describes superintelligent AI as hypothetical and possibly decades away, making its uncertain arrival part of why he wanted a concrete research target before leaving his existing work.

r002.rationale: He says he could not identify an actionable research program, but does not address the specific case of such AI arriving within twenty years.

r003.rationale: The response does not say that assuming a superintelligence can evade every safeguard makes proposed safeguards dismissible.

r004.rationale: The response does not discuss how precisely specifying a quantum computer enables mathematical study before a scalable machine exists.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I should say up front that I was never one of the people who thought the whole thing was ridiculous. I'd read Eliezer Yudkowsky's writings going back to the mid-2000s, and I actually found a lot of the core argument hard to dismiss. If you build something smarter than you that has goals different from yours, that seems like a bad situation to be in. Nothing about that struck me as crazy.

But I had a few different reasons for not dropping everything to work on it, and I want to separate them because they're really distinct.

The first was just a question of timing and tractability. Back in 2008 or 2010, if someone said "you should stop doing quantum complexity theory and work on AI alignment," my honest reaction was: work on what, exactly? There was no system in front of us to study. You could do philosophy about what a hypothetical superintelligence might want, you could prove theorems about idealized agents with utility functions, but it wasn't at all clear that any of that would connect to whatever actual AI eventually looked like. And in fact I think history vindicated that worry to some degree. The AI we got, large language models trained on the whole internet, looks almost nothing like the clean expected-utility-maximizer that a lot of that early theorizing assumed. A lot of careful thought went into agents that don't resemble GPT-4 at all.

The second reason was more about intellectual humility, or maybe suspicion of a certain kind of argument. There's a structure that goes: here's a chain of ten plausible-sounding premises, each one you'd assign maybe 80 or 90 percent to, and the conclusion is that this is the single most important problem in the history of the world and everything else is a rounding error. And I've learned to be wary of that. Not because any individual step is wrong, but because long chains of reasoning about the far future have a terrible track record, and because when the conclusion is "abandon your field and join my movement," you should at least check whether the argument is doing some motivated work. I didn't think the people making the argument were charlatans. I just thought the confidence level was way out of proportion to what anyone could actually know.

And the third reason, honestly, is that I think there's real value in people continuing to do the things they're good at. The world is not improved if every theoretical computer scientist becomes a mediocre alignment researcher. Comparative advantage is a real thing. I knew how to prove things about quantum computation. I did not know how to make a hypothetical future AI share human values, and neither did anyone else.

Now, what changed, and I'm happy to admit this changed, is that by 2022 the systems were actually here. You could poke at them. The question stopped being "what might a superintelligence want" and became "what is this specific thing doing and can we tell when it's lying to us." That's a scientific question. That's something I could imagine making progress on with the tools I have. So I spent a couple of years at OpenAI, and I don't regret it. But I'd still say my skepticism was about the "drop everything" framing, not about whether the problem was real. Those got conflated a lot, and I think they shouldn't have been.

r001.rationale: The candidate cites timing and the lack of a system to study, but does not identify uncertainty about when human-level or superhuman AI would arrive.

r002.rationale: The candidate questions what alignment researchers could work on before systems existed, but does not state that no actionable program existed even if such AI arrived within twenty years.

r003.rationale: The candidate does not discuss assuming a superintelligence could anticipate and circumvent every proposed safeguard.

r004.rationale: The candidate does not discuss how precisely specifying a quantum computer enables mathematical study of its capabilities before a scalable machine exists.

astra-6.text:
Well, I took the possibility seriously. What I was skeptical of was the leap from “this could be an enormous problem” to “therefore you should drop whatever you’re doing and work on it.” What, concretely, should you do? How would you tell whether you were making progress?

In theoretical computer science, I’m used to being confused, but I like having some way to turn that confusion into a precise question. With a lot of the arguments about superintelligence, I couldn’t see how to do that. You could construct a compelling story about disaster, but it was harder to identify a research task whose solution would demonstrably make that disaster less likely.

And there’s an opportunity cost. If someone is doing productive work on problems where they have real expertise, persuading them to abandon it requires more than pointing out that another problem has higher stakes. You need some reason to think that their switching will actually help. That was the part I wasn’t convinced of.

r001.rationale: The candidate questions whether proposed work would help, but says nothing about uncertainty over when human-level or superhuman AI might arrive.

r002.rationale: It says Aaronson could not identify research tasks that would demonstrably reduce the risk, but does not address the specific possibility of superintelligence arriving within twenty years.

r003.rationale: The candidate does not discuss safeguards being dismissed on the assumption that a superintelligence could anticipate and circumvent them.

r004.rationale: The candidate does not discuss specifying quantum computers or investigating their capabilities mathematically before building one.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I took the possibility of superintelligent AI seriously. What I was skeptical of was the leap from “this could be an enormously important problem” to “therefore, you should drop whatever you’re doing and work on it.” You also need some argument that you know what work would actually help.

If I’m working on quantum computing, I have concrete questions where I can make progress and check whether I’ve succeeded. With preventing an AI takeover, there seemed to be much less agreement about what constituted progress. How do you know that your proposed solution will make a future AI safer?

So I thought it was perfectly reasonable for some people to work on these questions. But the claim that everyone else was making a mistake by continuing their existing research—that seemed much harder to justify.
